Bill Loguidice wrote:
>>
In regards to the Retronicdesign USB controller adapter, [...] you need to reflash the adapter via USB for each different controller type you want to use. I'm definitely tempted, because it seems like an ideal solution to an otherwise unwieldly problem.
>>

This explanation makes sense.  I suppose that would "flash" the FPGA and allow the pins to be reconfigured to lead, well, where ever you need them to lead.

Another controller solution (that I just heard about today)-- not for the Astrocade, but for many other 8-bit systems-- is the "Ultimate PC Interface for the Intellivision and Colecovision. " It also provides support for the: Atari 2600 Joystick/Driving/Keypad, Atari 7800 ProLine Amiga/Commodore, Fairchild Channel F, Genesis, Magnavox Odyssey 2000 Sega Master System, TI-99, and 2014 Intv/Coleco Flashback:

http://www.intellivision.us/intvgames/interface/interface.php

Has anyone tried this adapter?

Adam

14262:
I finally got a chance to play George Moses' "Astro Zap 2000" last night using AstroBASIC.  I managed a score of:

Astro Zap 2000 - 26,250

I've attached a screenshot for reference.  Remember this is a BONUS game, it's worth just one point... but you earn that point easily-- just for playing the game and submitting ANY score.  Of course, you'll need a real Astrocade to do this because MAME doesn't support tape input.

Here are a few comments I've made about "Astro Zap 2000:"

1) It's must easier to be hit from the top or bottom of the screen because the invading missiles have less distance to travel to hit the fortress.

2) Once you start getting hit around a score of 20K, then you're game is going to end quite soon, as the missiles become VERY fast.  If you play the game anything like me, then you'll lose all of your men pretty-much right in a row.

3) If you have a good ear, then you might be able to play the game with your eyes closed!  That's because George made the missile's sound effect's pitch slightly different depending on which direction the missile is coming from.  Pretty neat.

4) Twice, while playing this game, I was destroyed by a missile coming from the right-side of the screen. I shot the missile, but instead of the missile being destroyed, the missile's sound effect pitch increased and the missile came faster!  I'm not sure if this is a bug or if it is meant to be part of the game.

5) I REALLY like that you don't need to point the controller AND press the button to fire in this game.  Just press the controller up, left, right or down and your fortress's missile fires in that direction.  Too bad "Space Fortress" doesn't play like this!  When playing "Space Fortress" your pressing that fire button constantly-- it wears me out.

The BASIC type-in program and instructions are here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_4/arcadian_vol_4_issue_09.pdf#Page=4

I've OCRed the instructions the the advice for typing the program into BASIC:

"ASTRO ZAP is similar to the commercial arcade game "SPACE ZAP" by Midway, only you don't need a quarter to play. It will keep score for up to four humans, using 1 hand control for each. When you RUN the program, input the number of players from the keypad. When the game starts you will use only the joystick to fire back at the invading missiles. No trigger is necessary. You will receive 250 points for each missile you eliminate. A Kamikaze will orbit your space fortress at random intervals. You must shoot it down before the second orbit or it will dive into you. Each human begins with three bases and will be awarded a bonus base every 10,000 points. As points accumulate the missiles will travel faster until you can no longer keep up with the onslaught. If the missile hits the base there will be a terrible explosion which goes on and on and on. If you get sick of watching yourself explode, pull the trigger to abort the fireworks. This will bring up the next player's turn. The only other use of the trigger is at the GAME OVER display if you wish to start a new game.

"IMPORTANT. Never put any spaces in this program unless you see the "[Space]" symbol. Any spaces you see are only in there for clarity. A word of caution about the letter "O" (as in OH). It is used as a variable in lines 21, 22, 101 and 510. Use care not to confuse it with the "0" (as in zero.) Also use the computer command word "INPUT" in line 500 instead of typing the word out. You should have 47 bytes of memory left, a minimum of 40 bytes are needed to handle the scorekeeping strings."

I'd be extremely pleased to see someone post a video of this game!

Go, AstroBASIC, go!

Adam

14273:
Ward wrote:
>>
typing in the "token'ized BASIC" version of the code (to steal terms from early Commodore computers)
>>

You're not stealing terms from Commodore, for AstroBASIC's keywords are also tokenized.  That's why keywords take up just one byte.  Most 8-bit BASICs are tokenized, aren't they?

>>
get us most of the way past the current "no tape loader in MESS" hurdle.
>>

The only truly useful way to get past the "'no tape loader in MESS' hurdle" would be to (surprise!) get tape support added into MAME.  Remember, MESS is no longer supported-- there's just MAME now.  The current version of MAME now supports the arcade games and the home consoles and computers.

>>
do a memory dump of a real machine, when it was running, mainly in that area reserved for AstroBasic, then perhaps we could hand-edit a "save state" (or similar) emulation file?
>>

I like Ward's idea-- it is VERY similar to creating a BASICart (run a BASIC program from cartridge).  However, the BIG drawback, is that each BASIC program would have to be re-done for MAME separately.  Adding tape support to MAME would only have to be done once.  Plus, if tapes were support in MAME, then programs could be created under emulation and saved to "tape" and then loaded on a real machine.  Remember, that although AstroBASIC was primarily used for BASIC programming, the tape interface can just as easily be used to load machine language programs.

"realpeterjack" pointed-out that save states vary from emulator to emulator.  Not only that, but save states are not guaranteed to be supported from one version of MAME to the next version of MAME.  A save state for the current version of MAME might only ever work in that version of MAME.

>>
Ignore this and continue on playing, though, if this is totally dumb/off-topic!!
>>

Ward, you forget-- for many of us, considering ideas like this IS a form of playing!  Also, talking about the Astrocade can't be off-topic in a Astrocade discussion group, can it?

Adam

14299:
A word of extreme caution!!!
Unplug your Bally / Astrocade unit EVERY TIME you get done using it!
Last night, while I was at this computer, which is right next to my work bench for Bally units, I heard a loud pop and the lights plugged into a strip dimmed for that instant. It was the plug-in power supply I use for testing the units! It was so hot, I couldn't unplug it right away! Had I not been here, it may have caught on fire and.....The unit was even turned OFF at the switch!!

Upon further evaluation, I looked at the schematic and found that there is 1 component across the terminals of the transformer even when the switch is off. It is C6, the huge electrolytic capacitor (10000 uF @ 10v).When I checked it out. it was a dead short. It seems it had dried up from being approximately 40 years old (I've known that feeling for 28 years)!So please unplug your unit each and every time to be safe!
Ken
14300:
That's a crazy story story, Ken.  I'm glad that you were home when your PS went kaput.  I had a similar experience with old computer equipment once.

I'd like to think that my house wouldn't have burned down had I not been home to unplug the monitor... but you never know.

Attached is a picture of the first level that I encountered in "The Incredible Wizard."  The levels are randomly selected, so it's just one of the, at least, 20 different map layouts that are available in the game.  Overlaid over the screenshot is a map of the Astrocade's screen locations.

The Astrocade's maximum screen resolution is 102x160 pixels.  Spectre systems created a screenmap graph paper layout that showed all 16,320 memory locations of the Astrocade's screen.  You can see that paper here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/astrocade_programming_sheets.pdf#page=4

Here is the same worksheet, as it was used to create the title screen for Spectre's "ICBM Attack" cartridge game:


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/spectre_systems/ICBM_Attack_concept_art/ICBM_Attack_02.jpg


This round's game for the Astrocade's High Score Club is "The Incredible Wizard."  I recreated the worksheet's graph paper layout for use with the Astrocade screenshots taken in MAME.  MAME's screenshot includes all of the Astrocade's overscan area of the screen, but the true resolution of the Astrocade is only what lays within the border of the graph paper.


As you can see in the picture, the bottom 11 lines of the screen are not displayed.  This allows these 440 bytes of Screen RAM (from $4F38 - $4FEF) to be used as scratchpad.  In addition to the 440 bytes of RAM that have been set aside for scratchpad by blanking the screen, there are also the 16 bytes of non-screen RAM (from $4FF0-$4FFF), giving to total of 454 bytes free RAM for the "Incredible Wizard" to work with.  Other games on the Astrocade, such as "Muncher," use blank areas of the screen for RAM.  Perhaps "Wizard" manages to scrape together a few more bytes of RAM using this method.

I had planned to use this picture of "The Incredible Wizard" to see if I could figure-out how the game drew the dungeon layouts, but now I doubt I'll use it for that reason.  Since the Astrocade High Score Club round ends tonight, I'll probably look into whatever game is up next to play.


I think the screen layout that I've attached is pretty neat.  Sometimes I make a posting like this and I wonder if I'm making sense to most (or even just some people).  Did most people understand what I was talking about in the post?

14326:
There are 3 things that can cause B&W instead of color:
1) The RF modulator is either going flaky or it's contacts need to be cleaned. I'm leaning towards the latter.
2) The Custom DATA chip is going out. This is the one that usually heats up and causes problems. It is located under the keypad. Good luck finding one of those for under $100.00! They are the rarest of all.
3) Your TV tuner is causing problems. If you move your unit quite often, sometimes the antenna or F connector (cable) gets intermittent.
You may try switching channels on your unit and TV. If that solves the problem, then your modulator is bad on the channel you were using. I have seen these modulators for sale on the internet. They are not listed as Bally or Astrovision. They are, however, or at least have been, commonly used. They usually can be acquired inexpensively. If you want to check out the inside of the modulator, you will need to slide it off the chassis, and pry the top piece of metal. If the chip inside (LM1889) is socketed, you can buy those in most electronics supply stores or on eBay.
Ken

Hi Ken,

Thanks very much for the explanation and tips!

I was able to confirm that the color output problem is with the RF modulator.  I did that by swapping out the RF modulator and replacing it with a working modulator from my other Astrovision console (that one works fine).  When I made the swap the Astrocade's output was immediately restored to color.

I suppose that's good news as it means none of the hard-to-find chips on the motherboard are bad.  I'll start poking around inside the modulator itself to see if I can isolate the bad part(s).  Hopefully it's just a bad cap or resistor or some other cheap part (there's a bunch of coils in there too, but they never seem to die of old age).
The LM1889 chip is socketed, so it should be easy enough to replace that part if necessary.

Thanks again for your help,

Paul

14331:
About the Black and White Astrocade, My Astrocade, a 2600, and an Odyssey 2 did that.   I sold an Astrocade thinking it wasn’t working to a repairman.   Then I got my Odyssey 2 to work.  It was because I was plugging it into a VCR and then through a Radio Shack brand Composite / S-Video inter-switcher / system selecotor to make a Laser Disc, a VHS,a Beta, and A DVD Player go into a DVD recorder via one S Video input.   Apparently some color in the RF gets lost in the translation the way it was hooked up when I outputted both S Video and Composite simultaneously, because it used a “powerless” converter.

Also I get a snowy picture when splitting an RF signal via RCA Y splitter and then running one to the CRT TV and the other to a DVD Recorder for recording.  The way to clear THAT up was to buy an RF Signal power booster/splitter.

Just throwing out some suggestions to check if it’s whether it’s splitting or combining and converting the signal.   Just make sure your TV setup isn’t making it black and white. Try a different RF System though the same TV Input and see if the TV only sees the Luma or not.  Also try fidgeting with your VHF TV tuner setting on your TV.

And I swear by retro TV adapters from Single RCA male to RF F Type.  You can use the RCA hole or plug in many of these consoles, and plug it straight without having to track down the specific RF Box.  The only thing that won’t work with is 4-port 5200s but I got the RF cable translated to single RCA Male and then from there used an RCA cord as an extension cord and plugged it into the TV the tradtional way.   You just had to reverse the genders on both connectors on the 5200 RF ”to TV” plug.

Don’t forget to use a VCR or analog RF DVD recorder.  That’s the cheapest way to record your video and hook it up to your TV.   No one uses analog TV anymore, hence, no need to switch to tv and game.

14333:
I think that your main problem all along is that you aren't impedance matching properly. When you just tie one output to several inputs, the impedance goes down drastically. The optimum impedance for a Bally/ Astrocade is 50 - 75 ohms.If you go lower or higher, the signal will have reflective regeneration and it will reduce the effective signal to each input. 2 @ 50 will look like 25 ohms if impedance. 3 will make it 16.667 ohms. That would drop the efficiency down in the mud. You either need to have an impedance matching network or daisy chain your units.Ken

Sorry, I was just explaining situations where all my RF systems were displaying B/W.  Without adding power, 1 Video out and 1 S Video out might have had a funny thing.   Also, If they are switchers, meaning only one is active at once, the impedence wouldn’t go down, It just went down when splitting into an Composite and S video output (each time only one input is connected) That caused a B/W.  This is becuase S Video is carried on a luma and chroma signal.     Also Splitting an RF signal before it reaches its destination caused snow.  That’s why all unpowered switches are passing physical switches.  Cheap, and if you just need one at  a time, all you need.

Also interestign enough, a Hauppauge rocket doesn’t work if the signal is split anywhere in the chain after a powered source.   I guess impedence is what the Haupapuge rocket uses for Sync, becuase it doesn’t recognize any signal when the RF of the Component is split after the last power.

I figured it out.   Just giving some advice on how I accidentally had a B/W sitch.  Trying to rule out my explanation before you worry about tinkering with the machine.
> On Apr 6, 2016, at 10:28 PM, ken lill kenzre@yahoo.com [ballyalley] <ballyalley@yahoogroups.com> wrote:

> I think that your main problem all along is that you aren't impedance matching properly. When you just tie one output to several inputs, the impedance goes down drastically. The optimum impedance for a Bally/ Astrocade is 50 - 75 ohms.If you go lower or higher, the signal will have reflective regeneration and it will reduce the effective signal to each input. 2 @ 50 will look like 25 ohms if impedance. 3 will make it 16.667 ohms. That would drop the efficiency down in the mud. You either need to have an impedance matching network or daisy chain your units.
> Ken

It's great that Lance is working on his game again.  The Astrocade High Score Club has rekindled my interest in programming the Astrocade too.  A few days ago, I started to muck about with my original "Nutting Manual" (officially known as the "Software and Hardware for the Bally Arcade - A Technical Description"). Proprietary Information
Dave Nutting Associates, Inc.
Do Not Reproduce


The watermark is written sideways, and is quite large.  If you have used the "Nutting Manual" before, then you're already aware of this.  These words obscure the pages.  My manual is an original manual from "Nutting Associates."  In this version of the book, the watermark is red (which turns black in the photocopies and scans that are currently online).  My manual also is in the original faux leather binder (that's kind of cute).  After much fumbling about in Photoshop to create a process to remove the watermark semi-automatically, I managed to remove it from every page of the manual.  Now the manual is easier to read.  This is especially helpful for the illustrations.  I printed and bound a copy yesterday.  I'm extremely pleased with it.  I'll be uploading a grayscale version of the "Nutting Manual" to BallyAlley.com after I create a proper pdf out of the hundreds of pages.

14341:
Brett said:

>>

We used a piece of red cellophane and a xerox machine to make 'clean' copies of the manual.

>>


It's funny that you say that, because that's what I was going to do if I couldn't come up with a way to remove the watermark from Photoshop: only I was going to use red cellophane and my flatbed scanner.  Once I figured out how to remove the red watermark in Photoshop, that wasn't necessary.  It took me a surprising long time to come up with a method that would work with EVERY page and could be made into a macro for the whole book.


To finally remove the watermark, I selected and then deleted all of the red in the image using "Color Range."  This left a sort of ghostly outline of the watermark that could still be read.  To remove the outline, I selected the red channel from the RGB image.  This channel, against what you'd think, doesn't show the red in the image.  So, effectively, the watermark (mostly) disappeared.  I then changed the image to grayscale with the red channel selected.  In this mode, grayscale actually discards the two other channels (Blue and Green), which left a grayscale image is easy to read.  Then I messed about with the brightness and contrast until I got an image that I was happy with.  This worked best for the proper "Nutting manual" (the first 143 pages of the book).  This method also worked for the source code listing in the back of the book, but the source code came out much lighter due to remnants of the watermark were left behind if I didn't lighten the page more.


Adam

This impedance discussion is interesting, but doesn't apply to my situation.

As I mentioned in my original post, the console's output would sometimes display in color but other times display in black and white.  In all cases I have the console connected through the Bally game/TV switch, then through a 300-to-75 ohm adapter to the TV's ANT input.

I recently tried bypassing the game/TV switch by connecting the console directly to the TV's ANT input though an RCA-female-to-F-type-male adapter.  It made no difference (the Bally console's output continues to display in B&W; the Astrovision console displays in color.  (I might add that the output is a bit cleaner, with less noise, using the adapter instead of the switch.)

Since I've now isolated the problem to the RF modulator box in the Bally console (by swapping it with the known good RF modulator box from my Astrovision console), and since the LM1889 chip in both RF modulator boxes is socketed, I intend to next try swapping the chips to see if the chip is the problem (hopefully it is, so I can then easily replace it (lots of new and used LM1889's listed on eBay).

Thanks again for everyone's explanations and suggestions.

14355:
I wrote an article called "Programming the Bally Arcade/Astrocade."  I wrote this, mostly to completion, back in 2012.  It wasn't until the Astrocade High Score Club peaked my interest again in programming the Bally Arcade system that I decided that it was time to finish and polish the article so that others could use it.

This article explains how to set up the "PS Pad" text editor so that it will automatically assemble the source code of a program that runs on the Zilog Z80 CPU of the Bally Arcade/Astrocade. We'll be using the "Zmac" z80 cross-assembler, which is a command line-only program.

More specifically, you'll be guided through the process required to make "Zmac" the default editor for assembling Bally Arcade/Astrocade programs. Once these step-by-step directions are completed, "PS Pad" will be more than just a text editor; it will become a nearly complete Integrated Development Environment (IDE).

Here is what is covered in this article:

1.  Introduction
2.  Astrocade Programming Using the "Nutting Manual"
3.  Download the "Zmac" Assembler
4.  Download "PS Pad" and z80.ini
5.  Download the "Home Video-Game Library" Equates (HVGLIB.H)
6.  Set Up "PS Pad" for Use with the "Zmac" Assembler
7.  Test "PS Pad" by Assembling Z80 Source Code
8.  Summary

My friend Chris, who isn't an assembly language programmer, was this article's test subject (i.e. guinea pig).  He followed all of the steps in the article.  When he was done, he was able to assemble the cartridge"Treasure Cove" from its source code.  Hooray!  Than, because he is awesome (!), he edited the article to make sure it was easy enough for a beginner to follow.  Thanks for the help, Chris.  You rule!

You can read "Programing the Bally Arcade/Astrocade," here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html#ProgrammingTheBallyArcade-Astrocade

I am especially interested in hearing feedback from anyone who follows these directions.

Enjoy!

Adam
14356:
I have added Software and Hardware for the Bally Arcade - A Technical Description (unofficially, but commonly, called the "Nutting Manual") to archive.org.  This is a 179MB grayscale version of the manual that has had the red watermark removed from all of the pages.  The manual describes the Bally Home Video-Game System. The description begins with a discussion of the major sub-sections of the system. Following this, each sub-section is presented in greater detail. The particulars include sequence-calling and resource use.


The major sub-sections of the system are:

  1.  The User Program Interface - Allows cartridges to reference the system routines through a standard interface. Includes an interpreter.
  2.  The Screen Handler - A complex set of routines for creating
screen images. Includes facilities for initialization, pattern and
character display, coordinate conversion, and object vectoring.
  3.  The Interrupt Processor - Decrements timers, plays music and produces sounds.
  4.  The Human Interface - Reads keyboard and control handles, and inputs game selection and options.
  5.  Math Routines - A package of routines for manipulating floating BCD numbers.

Also included in the "Nutting manual" are the complete source-code listings for the console's four built-in programs (Calculator, Checkmate, Gunfight and Scribbling).


The manual can be downloaded here:


https://archive.org/details/SoftwareAndHardwareForTheBallyArcadeATechnicalDescriptionDaveNuttingAssociates


I expected there to be a preview of the manual available after I uploaded it to Archive.org, but one doesn't exist.  It's possible that it takes time to be created.  In the meantime, even if you can't preview the document, you can download the pdf from there and use it on your computer.

The description begins with a discussion of the major sub-sections of the system. Following this, each sub-section is presented in greater detail. The particulars include sequence-calling and resource use.
The major sub-sections of the system are:

   - The User Program Interface - Allows cartridges to reference the system routines through a standard interface. Includes an interpreter.
   - The Screen Handler - A complex set of routines for creating
screen images. Includes facilities for initialization, pattern and
character display, coordinate conversion, and object vectoring.
   - The Interrupt Processor - Decrements timers, plays music and produces sounds.
   - The Human Interface - Reads keyboard and control handles, and inputs game selection and options.
   - Math Routines - A package of routines for manipulating floating BCD numbers.
Also included in the "Nutting manual" are the complete source-code listings for the console's four built-in programs (Calculator, Checkmate, Gunfight andScribbling).
The manual can be downloaded here:

https://archive.org/details/SoftwareAndHardwareForTheBallyArcadeATechnicalDescriptionDaveNuttingAssociates
I expected there to be a preview of the manual available after I uploaded it to Archive.org, but one doesn't exist.  It's possible that it takes time to be created.  In the meantime, even if you can't preview the document, you can download the pdf from there and use it on your computer.
Adam

I created "Astrocade Screen Layout: 102 x 160 Graph Paper" based on similar graph paper designed by Spectre Systems in the early 1980s.

Use Bally Arcade/Astrocade screenshots taken from the Astrocade emulator included with MAME to create screen layouts on "graph paper." These can then be used to help understand how an Astrocade program functions (such as how the screen is built or laid-out). Included are several graphic files that require a graphics editor (such as Photoshop or GIMP) that can deal with TIFF files that have layers. Instructions explain how to combine a screenshot as a separate layer on the "graph paper."


You can read more about it here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html#AstrocadeScreenLayoutGraphPaperGraphicFile


Here are the instructions on how to use the TIFF "graph paper:"


"Astrocade Screen Layout: 102 x 160 Graph Paper"
By Adam Trionfo
April 12, 2016


I)  Summary
    -------

This documentation explains how to use Bally Arcade/Astrocade screenshots taken from the Astrocade emulator included with MAME to create screen layouts that can be used to help understand how an Astrocade program functions (such as how the screen is built).


II)  Required: Files and Graphics Editor
     -----------------------------------

This documentation is included in an archive with the following files:

1) Astrocade Screen Layout - 102 x 160 Graph Paper (Cropped)(With Layers).tif
2) Astrocade Screen Layout - 102 x 160 Graph Paper (Doc).txt
3) Incredible Wizard (Astrocade Screen Layout)(Graph Paper 102 x 160).gif
4) Incredible Wizard - Level 001 (Enlarged).png
5) Incredible Wizard - Level 001 (Small).png

The user is presumed to be able to open and manipulate at least four different graphic files: TIF (with layers), JPG, GIF and PNG.  A quality graphics editor, such as Photoshop or GIMP, is required.


III)  Graph Paper and the Astrocade's Screen Layout
      ---------------------------------------------

The Bally Arcade/Astrocade's maximum screen resolution is 102 x 160 pixels.  To help create graphics for the console, Spectre Systems created special graph paper in the early 1980s that simulated the Astrocade's screen layout.  It showed all 16,320 memory locations of the Astrocade's screen.  You can view the graph paper created by Spectre here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/astrocade_programming_sheets.pdf#page=4

Notice the left-side of the graph paper has four-digit hexadecimal numbers placed every ten lines.  These digits are the memory addresses of the Astrocade's Screen RAM.  The top-left square is memory address $4000.  Line 101's first memory address is $4FA0.  The last byte of memory in Screen RAM is $4FEF (the bottom-right square).  More information about the Astrocade's screen layout is available in the book "Software and Hardware for the Bally Arcade - A Technical Description" (aka "Nutting Manual" and/or "The Handbook of Hardware & Software").

Here is an example of the the Spectre graph paper in use.  This graph paper was used to create the title screen for Spectre's cartridge game called "ICBM Attack."

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/spectre_systems/ICBM_Attack_concept_art/ICBM_Attack_02.jpg

As you can see from the above picture, Spectre used their graph paper to draw a screen.  This picture was then translated to data for the program and used as the game's title screen.  However, we're going to be working in reverse: taking a screenshot (completed graphics) and placing it onto graph paper.


IV)   Astrocade Graph Paper: 21'st Century Style
      ------------------------------------------

Using Photoshop CS2, I recreated a worksheet (graph paper) layout for use with the Astrocade screenshots taken in the Astrocade emulation in MAME.  Screenshots taken using MAME include all of the Astrocade's overscan area of the screen, but the true resolution of the Astrocade is ONLY what lies within the border of the graph paper.  The re-created graph paper in this archive is called:

Astrocade Screen Layout (Graph Paper 102 x 160)(Cropped)(With Layers).tif

The Astrocade Screen Layout uses five layers, plus a background.

The dimensions of this graph paper are:

DPI    -  720/inch
Width  -  7040 pixels
Height -  4800 pixels
Width  -  9.778 inches
Height -  6.667 inches

A screenshot in MAME is saved as a PNG with these dimensions:

DPI    -  72/inch
Width  -  352 pixels
Height -  240 pixels
Width  -  4.889 inches
Height -  3.333 inches

For an example of a MAME screenshot, open and view the picture "Incredible Wizard - Level 001 (Small).png"

The general idea to make this screenshot more useful is to take the screenshot from MAME, resize it, and paste it onto the recreated Astrocade layout graph paper.  The MAME screenshot will be pasted "below" the grid of the graph paper; therefore, the screenshot will appear "behind" the grid of blue lines that makes the graph paper.

(Note that these instructions will give you a general idea of how to use the Astrocade graph paper, but these are not step-by-step directions-- a familiarity with graphic editors is required here.)

Here's how to resize an image in Photoshop (hopefully these tips will help people who use other graphics editors, like GIMP).  First, open up the example found in the archive called "Incredible Wizard - Level 001 (Small).png."
Follow these directions to create a screenshot:

1) Change the image size.

2) Make sure "Constrain Proportions" is clicked.

3) Set "Resample Image" to "Nearest Neighbor."  The default is "bicubic--" you DON'T want that, as it will blur your image when it is resized.

4) Change "Resolution to 720."  As long as "Constrain Proportions" is clicked, this will automatically change the Height to 2400 pixels and Width to 3520 pixels.

5) Now change Height to 4800 pixels.  This will automatically change Width to 7040 pixels.

6) With these changes made, the screenshot is exactly the same size as the "graph paper."

7) Now select the entire screenshot and copy it as a new layer directly under the layer called "Grid" on the "Graph Paper."

8) The screenshot should fill the entire "graph paper" perfectly.  Anything outside of the graph paper's blue outline is the Astrocade's screen's overscan area.

9) Your finished picture should look like the included image called "Incredible Wizard (Astrocade Screen Layout)(Graph Paper 102 x 160).gif"

Now that we've gone and placed a screenshot on graph paper, let's take advantage of what we can do with it.


V)    Learning from Resized Screenshots on "Graph Paper"
      --------------------------------------------------

As you can see in the resized picture, the bottom 11 lines of the screen are not displayed (the color of these lines in "The Incredible Wizard" screenshot has been changed to black-- just like the overscan area).  This allows these 440 bytes of Screen RAM (from $4F38 - $4FEF) to be used as scratchpad.  In addition to the 440 bytes of RAM that have been set aside for scratchpad by blanking the screen, there are also the 16 bytes of non-screen RAM (from $4FF0-$4FFF), giving to total of 454 bytes free RAM for the "Incredible Wizard" to work with.  Other games on the Astrocade, such as "Muncher," use blank areas of the screen for RAM.  Perhaps "Wizard" manages to scrape together a few more bytes of RAM using this method.

I had planned to use this picture of "The Incredible Wizard" to see if I could figure-out how the game drew the dungeon layouts, but now I doubt that I'll use it for that reason (I've moved onto other projects).

Pasting MAME screenshots onto the "Astrocade Screen Layout Graph Paper" will allow you to use MAME screenshots in new ways.  You'll soon learn that there is a lot of power in know exactly what the screen RAM layout looks like when a picture is displayed on it.  Try using the screenshot/graph paper combination with a Z80 disassembler (such as "DZ80").  This will allow you to figure-out how a program draws and lays out a screen much easier.

Until next time, Astrocade fans... Keep Buggin'

14368:
I added a review, by  Kevin O'Neill, of the cartridge game "Mazeman."  This review was originally published in the newsletter NIAGARA B.U.G. BULLETIN, 2, no. 5 (June 1984): 22.

This game was released in 1984 by Dave Caron (but, according to Mike White, was not programmed by him).  Rather than quote the review, here is some information from an ad for the game:

"MAZEMAN is unlike any 'gobble game' you have ever seen! Each time you clear a screen, you find yourself beginning a different maze. There are 12 completely different mazes, each requiring changes in tactics. [...] The four bad guys get slightly faster and a bit more aggressive with each new maze. The mazes cycle after 12, but the increase in difficulty goes on and on. From level one through nine there are eight "Jekyl to Hyde" transformers per maze. After level 9 there are only four. MAZEMAN has challenge enough for the serious gamer, but will provide hours of satisfaction for the beginner."

You can read the full review, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/reviews/reviews.html#MazemanReviewKevinONeill

I spent some time this morning playing this 4K game to get some screenshots for the review.  The game is quite fun-- I recommend it.  I may even end up choosing it for the Astrocade High Score Club next round.

Enjoy!

Adam

Should I Number these? post to the same thread, or start again each time...

Anyway,

I decided to start from the bottom of the code and work my way up, as it seems most of the subroutines are down there.

Not yet sure what the first few routines I passed were doing. I was looking for the draw routines anyway.

I noticed the use of XOR A for fast setting A to 0, so was commenting them as I went up.

Then I ran into this:

;  Following the code...

;    1)  $4F59 = $3A06  ($3A06 holds $0310)

;    2)  $4F5B = $00

;    3)  COL3L = $63 (Red)

I'm still not sure what Adam meant at 1) but 3) caught my interest and I looked over the entire block and the comments already there.

Just trying to follow this block I'm learning and re-learning Z80. (how much I've forgotten...)

I've actually ended up re-writing my comments 3 times as I began to better understand what was going on here.

My copy of wizwor.asm in this section now reads:

;  Following the code...

;    1)  $4F59 = $3A06  ($3A06 holds $0310)

;    2)  $4F5B = $00

;    3)  COL3L = $63 (Red)

L3D32:  EXX

        LD      HL,$3A06	; HL=3A06

        LD      ($4F59),HL      ; Set 4F59 to $3A06

        LD      HL,$4F5B	; HL=4F5B

        LD      (HL),$00        ; 4F5B=0 Why? Zeroed in LDIR ...


L3D3E:  LD      A,$63           ; $63 is the color red

        OUT     (COL3L),A       ; COLor 3 Left = $63 (Color Red)

        LD      A,$F5           ; F5 is the color Light Blue

        OUT     (COL1L),A       ; COLor 1 Left = $F5 (Light Blue)

        LD      HL,$4F42

        SET     7,(HL)          ; Set Most Significant Bit of $4F42

        INC     HL              ; Set HL to $4F43

        XOR     A               ; Change A to $00

        LD      (HL),A          ; $4F43 = 0

        OUT     (COL0L),A       ; write COLor 0 Left = $00 (Black)

        INC     A               ; A = $01

        LD      HL,$4F66        ;

        LD      (HL),A          ; $4F66 = $01

        LD      HL,($4F59)      ; Value could be 3A06 from L3D32...
				; or something else
				; if entered from L3D3E

        PUSH    HL              ; Save value on stack

        LD      HL,$4F44        ; Start of block

        LD      BC,$0021	; Count

        LD      (HL),$00        ; $4F44 = $00 Zero first entry.

        LD      E,L             ; E = $44

        LD      D,H             ; D = $4F

        INC     DE              ; DE = $4F45 Same block +1

        LDIR                    ; Zero Block
				; LD (DE),(HL) INC DE,HL DEC BC
				; Repeat to BC=0
				; In Effect Copy 4F44-4F65 to 4F45-4F66.
				; Since 4F44 was zeroed it just
				; clears 4F45-4F66.

        LD      HL,$4F59

        LD      BC,$0818	; Load B Count 08 and
				; C port 18 (Sound Block Transfer)

        OTIR    		; OUT(c),(HL) INC HL DEC B until B=0.
				; Since 4F59-4F61 are now 0 this clears
				; all sound ports to 0

        POP     HL		; Get value from stack

        LD      ($4F59),HL	; put here again. Saved from wipe.

        EXX

        RET


Basically, the first entry point (L3D32) Sets 2 values in RAM then falls through to the second entry point.

There is sets some colour values, sets a bit on a memory address (4F43) and saves one of the addresses in the 4F44-4F66 block before zeroing the block. Once zeroed, it uses the block to zero the sound ports.
Having done that, it restores the saved value to the now zeroed block.

At first I coulden't figure out why they would set a value in the block, move it to stack, zero the block then move the value back.

Then I realized I was forgetting the second entry point. If the second entry point is used that value could be entirely different.

Still not sure why they would zero 4F5B and set 4F66 to 1 when they are about the zero the entire 4F45-4F66 block.

Didn't comment the EXX as I think I know what that does.

Sorry it's not more exciting.

14378:
I updated the "Machine Language Manager' review by Bob Fabris and Al Rathmell.  This review was originally published in ARCADIAN 4, no. 3 (Dec. 24, 1981): 29.  Previously, it was only available as a scanned pdf, but now it has been OCRed and made into it's own webpage with several images have been added to spruce-up the review, plus there are related links now available.

The "Machine Language Manager" (MLM) cartridge was released by The Bit Fiddlers (Andy Guevara).  The "MLM" is a machine language monitor that allows an un expanded, 4K Bally Arcade/Astrocade to program in machine language using hex digits instead of the clumsy decimal method that is required by "Bally BASIC" and "AstroBASIC."


Lance's continued work on the disassembly of "The Incredible Wizard" inspired me to take another look at the review and the manual:


http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/reviews/reviews.html#MachineLanguageManagerReview


Have fun!


Adam

Mazeman is the main game for Round 6 of the Astrocade High Score Club. Round 6 will last two weeks. The round ends on Sunday, May 1'st at 8pm MST.

"Mazeman"

"Mazeman" is a maze game, but it's not exactly a "Pac-Man" clone (like the officially unreleased, yet much more common, Muncher). This very rare third-party game was released by Dave Carson in 1984, but it was not programmed by him. Mike White, in the Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ wrote, "The programmer of this cartridge wanted to remain anonymous for fear of legal troubles." While on a phone call with Mike, in about 2001, he told me that the Mazeman was programmed by a man for his kids. To this day, I'm not sure who created Mazeman-- which is a shame, as it plays very well and is quite fun.


Read the details for this round on the HSC in the AtariAge forums:


http://atariage.com/forums/topic/251688-hsc01-round-6-mazeman/


Note that no BASIC bonus game has been picked yet.  I'm looking for ideas (see the above post for details).


Come an play Mazeman with the rest of us.  Hope to see ya there!


Adam

I always get a kick out of people taking photos of their items on the ground, it just blows my mind that people put these things on concrete, asphalt and grass instead of taking pictures indoors on a nice, clean surface. 
What I like about this auction is the fact that I am now 100% convinced that the wheels were in fact sold with the cartridge at one point, but unfortunately we have never seen the original packaging.  All the wheels I have came from Bally sealed in a bag, and the only wheel I bought in the wild was much like this one, included with a Bally system (in fact it was installed on one of the controllers).
Definitely a neat bit of history and I guess you could call this the rarest Bally accessory ever made. 
-Michael  128kgames.com 128K. Your Life Will Never Be The Same.

I'm happy to announce that my code to add RAM expansions has been accepted into MESS. It works basically the same as before, but uses more of MESS's own functions and macros. In a way, this makes code easier to write, since some things get taken care of behind the scene. But there was also more of a learning curve than just using C, which I was already familiar with. It may be awhile before the next official version gets released. In the meantime, anyone can compile from the public SVN. Or if you don't want to compile your own, there are automatically compiled daily builds on this site:

http://bobz38.free.fr/mess_autobuild/index.php

To use this, start the Astrocade in MESS and hit tab to bring up the MESS menu. Then, go to dip switches to change the system configuration. There are a number of RAM expansions to choose from, as well as the switch to write protect the RAM (make it treated like ROM). Once you have the configuration you want, hit F3 to do a soft reset. You can change the RAM write protect switch at any time, but you should always do a reset after changing the RAM expansion. If you start a cart with a RAM expansion already saved in your configuration file, or switch to a different cart, you may also need to do a soft reset (as with ICBM Attack) to get the cart to start.

This allows you to run extended BASIC carts, and set and read any memory area in the RAM expansion. You can also set and read the extended memory area addressable by Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC. I have not, at this time, attempted to add the INS8154 chip to the Blue RAM expansion. I also have not added the 2K/6K switch. I'd need tape loading support to test it practically. Perhaps the next thing to look at is fixing cartridge swapping, which would allow BASICarts requiring a RAM expansion to run in MESS.

If anyone tries this out, let me know what you think.

Paul

I have updated the Bally Arcade/Astrocade ROM set.  I haven't added any new files, nor have I renamed any of the files in the TOSEC directory.  However, at some point in one of the updates of MESS/MAME, the names of the expected ROMs have changed for some of the programs.  I have renamed these ROMs to reflect what MAME now expects them to be when it loads them.

Also, the MAME ROM files have now been individually zipped.  This means that you can now simply rename the directory in the ROM archive called "mame" to "roms" and then place the newly renamed "roms" directory into your MAME directory.  Now, you'll be able to load up all of the ROMs from within MAME without any hitches.

As always, the Astrocade ROM collection is available here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/cart_images.html#AstrocadeROMCollection

Hopefully, this new ROM set will allow people to use the Astrocade emulator in MAME a little easier.

It's still in there, though options like that got moved around a bit with the merger with MAME. Hit TAB, then select "Slot Devices". Hit the left and right arrows to choose an option under "exp" for the expansion you want, then arrow down to "Reset" and hit enter to mount it. Select a compatible cartridge (i.e. ViperSOFT Expansion / VIPERSoft BASIC), and it should run. Once the expansion is mounted, you can select "Machine Configuration" from the TAB menu to flip any switches that have been defined, like the RAM write protect switch.

Bally Pin (later called Astrocade Pinball) is the main game for Round 7 of the Astrocade High Score Club. I'll be out of town when a two-week round would normally end, so this round will last an extra week. It's either that, or make the round a week shorter (which I don't want to do). For this reason, Round 7 will last three weeks. The round ends on Sunday, May 22'nd at 8pm MST.

Bally Pin


"It has everything except a slot to collect your quarters! Thumper bumpers! Kicker targets! Drop targets! Realistic flipper action! They'll even catch the ball and roll it back and forth to give you the direction you want! Two different playing fields create the impression of having two pinball machines in one. Up to 4 players."

I refer to this game as Bally Pin (since the game's name was not renamed on the re-released Astrocade Pinball). Bally Pin is a 4K game, originally released in 1979, by Bally. This game was programmed by Bob Ogden and Scot L. Norris (who provided sound effects, as he did for many of Bally's game cartridges).

The Bally Pin cartridge ROM image (called "ballybin.bin") is part of this archive:


http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/cart_images.html#AstrocadeROMCollection


One hint: when I played Bally Pin under emulation, I setup the left and right Shift keys to be the flippers (I had to turn off "Sticky keys" under Windows, as it activates if you press shift five times in a row).

The Astrocade version of the "Bally Pin" manual is here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/cart_manuals/pdf_manuals/Bally_Pin_%28instructions%29%28bally%29%28a1%29%28color%29%28300%20dpi%29.pdf


The Bally version of the "Bally Pin" manual is here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/cart_manuals/pdf_manuals/bally%20pin%20%28instructions%29%28bally%29%28color%29%28300%20dpi%29.pdf


Here is a video review of "Bally Pin" by "Nice and Games:"


https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gIyTG9xUd9s&feature=youtu.be


Bill Kunkel's and Arnie Katz's "Arcade Alley" department in Video magazine has a column called Astrovision's Rising Star in the May 1982 issue. There is a short review of Bally Pin in the article. I've extracted it here:

"Bally Pin (Astrovision/3005) waited in limbo for some time before seeing the light of day. Its year or more of obscurity proved undeserved. This is absolutely the best video-game pinball simulation ever offered for any programmable home system. It clearly shows Bally's expertise in the pinball area. It had to be first class all the way to maintain Bally's reputation, and is.

"Designer Bob Ogdon responded to the challenge with a dual-playfield masterpiece that captures all the sights, sounds, and spirit of genuine flipper-game play. Using a pair of the Professional Arcade's excellent pistol-grip command units, players can effectively control left- and right-side flippers individually. Both of the electronic tables use the same flipper arrangement. Each has a pair of bats at the center of the bottom of the screen, with single flippers guarding two extra drains located along the lower edge of the field to the left and right of the central pair.

"The trimmings should be familiar to those who occasionally forsake the delights of Pac-Man and Defender for coin-op pinball machines. The highlights include back bumpers, thumper bumpers, drop targets, a spinner, and virtually everything else you'd expect except a flashing back-plate.

"Orchestrating ball movement is perhaps the hardest part of pinball to translate to the video screen. Bill Budge, who created the best-selling Apple II program Raster Blaster, worked out the ball dynamics mathematically, determining the effect of gravity and other physical laws on the trajectory of a wildly bouncing metal sphere. Bob Ogdon has done virtually as well here, infusing his creation with a feeling of realism that is generally absent in video pin contests.

"Field number one in Bally Pin is a colorful explosion of white, red, and yellow. The second table is equally vibrant, though many will find its more soothing dark field easier on the eyes. Drop targets and bumpers are placed a little differently in each version, though they are the same overall.

"Standard pinball strategy definitely applies, so gaining optimal control over flipper movement is the top priority. The flippers can be held in the up position indefinitely, permitting the arcader to trap the ball for a few seconds while deciding which part of the field should be its next destination. Having the player hold one controller in each hand is this game's most significant innovation. It provides a sensation unlike anything else in video-gaming while faithfully reproducing the necessary pinball ambience."

The full article can be read here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/articles_and_news/articles_and_news.html#AstrovisionsRisingStar


Bally Pin play settings for the Astrocade High Score Club are:

Unlike many Bally games, Bally Pin has no play settings. As usual, 10 points can be earned this round (excluding bonus points). You can earn up to 5 points for playing the first table ("Bally Pin I") and 5 more points for playing the second table ("Bally Pin II").

"Bally Pin" Bonus Points

I couldn't think of many ways to earn bonus points for Bally Pin. Keeping track of how many points you score for your first ball seems most obvious, but it seems hard to keep track of this score during the game. If you have any other ideas for bonus points for this game, then let me know. Currently, there are two ways to score bonus points (neither is easy) for Bally Pin:

1) Bally Pin I - Beat 320,430 points - Don Gladden scored 320,430 points on "Bally Pin I" (ARCADIAN 6, no. 3 (Jan. 27, 1984): 23.)  Beat Don's score.

2) Bally Pin II - Beat 336,700 points - Stan Kendall scored 336,700 points on "Bally Pin II" (ARCADIAN 6, no. 2 (Dec. 22, 1983): 14.)  Beat Stan's score.


"Avalanche!" (BASIC Bonus Game)


Paul did such a great job choosing Candy Man for the last round (that was fun game!). I figured it was worth asking him privately for a suggestion for this round's BASIC bonus game. He replied to me by saying, "Avalanche! by Steve Walters came to mind. It's kind of like a strategy Pachinko game--pretty unique. I don't have time to try it again tonight, but maybe it will suit you." Well, I tried the game this evening. The game isn't fast (it's not meant to be), but it seems to provide what I like best about Bally BASIC programs: it is a game for the Astrocade that probably never would have been created if Steve Walters didn't (I surmise) have some interest in the game pachinko.



I don't quite get the scoring in Avalanche!... but we'll work it out during the round (I hope).

There are some very brief instructions for the game from an ad in Summer 1982 Sourcebook: "Avalanche! - Try to drop a ball in the top without making any balls fall past the levers to the bottom. After a few turns, someone will cause an avalanche! For 1 to 4 players."

Avalanche! Bonus Points

1) Playing Avalanche! - You get a bonus point just for playing Avalanche!

2) Avalanche! High Score - You can earn another bonus point if you get the highest score for this game.

3) Video of Avalanche! - To continue to promote Astrocade BASIC programs, a bonus point will be awarded to the first person to upload a video of Avalanche! containing a full game, plus the game's loading screen.

4) Avalanche! Play Instructions - The person who explains how the rules for this game work will receive a bonus point. This is a competition of sorts. If more than one person explains the rules, then the winner will be whoever writes the rules up best (in my opinion).

Sorry that I don't have more information to provide for Avalanche! (hopefully someone can help out here).

Please post all of your scores for both games here. Scores posted on the Bally Alley discussion group will no longer be accepted. If you post a video score, then please note the score obtained in the video-- as this makes it easier for me to keep track of all the scores.


Be sure to post all scores for this game in the AtariAge forums:


http://atariage.com/forums/topic/252219-hsc01-round-7-bally-pin-pinball/


Enjoy playing Bally Pin and discovering Avalanche!


Adam

14418:
This is the Astrocade Chuck, not the Atari 2600, ColecoVision, Vectrex etc.  :)  
Unfortunately we're not the most popular console out there (God knows why) so 3rd party support for the system has been lacking as of late.  Back in the day, that's a different story: look at all the tapes, cartridges, newsletters and add ons that were built.  
Unfortunately today I don't know if you've got enough working systems out there to draw enough interested people into the scene who would want to make items for it.  Plus there's that bad reputation of console failure, even if its warranted.  Even if you do find one I'm thinking some people might be too afraid to take the chance of using it.  (That's why so many of us diehards have multiple spares).   
Ken's RAM add on was great to have, as was his multi-carts.  Plus I know he had a hand (I believe) in adapting the multi-cart PCB for the last few releases of Crazy Climber and I think WAR?  (Guys correct me if I am wrong here). 
As far as things like the S-VIDEO adapter go those weren't "new" in the sense they were just made, those things were created back in 2006-2007 if memory servers, and I only picked up the last of the stock a few years ago.  
If by new S-VIDEO supplier you mean console5.com unless you heard differently they are out of the remaining S-VIDEO boards I sold them; I am not aware of them moving forward with creating new boards.  If that's the case, fantastic, and a great addition to the cap kits they sell. 
As someone who has been pushing his own collaborative Astrocade project for years I can tell you no matter how much you may want something it doesn't mean its going to happen.  Unfortunate, but thats life. 
-Michael  128kgames.com 128K. Your Life Will Never Be The Same.

14420:
I'm an EM pinball guy who enjoys vintage computers (not really a gamer, but I love the Astrocade and the Atari 800), but I have been looking under the hood on this system and thinking about what I could do to mod this system to make it less finicky. What kills me is that I owned a half dozen systems that I had working perfectly, but a fire claimed 5 of them and a 6th died and the machines out there to buy that actually are fixable are either selling for way too much money, or are not worth trying to fix. I do have 2 systems, but one of them has major color issues (needs new rf) and a second gets hot very fast.
I am sure this topic has been discussed ad nauseum, but when I opened up the console with the color issues, I noticed that the rf has a short in and that the box is mounted very close to the front on the unit, meaning if I want to solder in the new rf box (already purchased) and install a new rf cable, I need to either drill a hole in the front of the unit to feed the new cable, or cut down the cord and deal with a degraded image.
The second issue is the overheating problem. There is definitely dead space in the console. What would it take to install a fan to deal with the heat issues this system is notorious for?
I'm also not really a fan of S video since none of my TVs or monitors have it. Is there a (ideally for a CRT) composite mod and is anyone out there playing with the idea of a SCART or HDMI mod for the unit (for HDTVs)? I'm not really a fan of playing older game systems on a modern TV as the lag issue and graphics display terribly, but it'd be an interesting topic to explore.
Sorry if these questions sound silly or have been answered already. I've been a member of this newsgroup for about 12 years, but haven't looked at every post over those years.
--John M

14421:
Hi John,
Thank you for your recent order.
First off, the modulator you bought should be a drop in, if you got the Aztec UM1291-1. Yes, it is close to the front of the machine, but from the start, Bally and Astrovision both used standard 75 ohm coax. (50 ohm will work also.) and they bent it sharply right out of the RCA plug. You will need to have an end that doesn't have any plastic covering the RCA jack. It must be a plain RCA plug with a long pin.
As far as the heat problem, I would suggest that you get a cheap laptop fan system and put it under the Bally. Buy a cheap phone charger that has the same type plug in it as does the fan. those fans are 5V, just like the chargers. They work great.
I can build you a comp video ( like one on a VCR ) system that has comp video and pseudo-stereo sound. Both sides are actually the same output just separate from each other. you will need a 3 section AV RCA cable (Yellow for video, red for right audio and white for left audio). You will have to solder it in on the modulator pins. You will need to replace the modulator to get color out. Without it you will only get black and white. Cost is $30.00 with free shipping and handling..

Hardly anyone has original RAM upgrades for the Astrocade.  I personally only know of a few people that own the Viper, Blue Ram unit or 64K RAM boards.  Ken Lill and Mike White designed and built the 32K upgrade "Lil' White Ram" (cute name) back in 2008.  I own that upgrade (just used it a couple of days ago!).  I also own a 16K Blue Ram unit, although Paul Thacker has that now for tape archiving purposes.
Ken, how many Lil' White Rams did you sell?

I presume that Chuck asked how many people own Astrocades (and RAM upgrades for it) because it seems nearly absurd to post reviews of software that most people can't evenuse.  I figure, the more people that know about the software for the Astrocade that requires RAM upgrades, then the more chances that someone will add tape support to the Astrocade emulator in MAME.   The emulator already supports RAM upgrades-- although it doesn't support the Blue Ram's 8154 I/O chip.

On December 21, 2015, Adam wrote:
>>
I added five 300-Baud Bally BASIC Programs to BallyAlley.com:

1) "Plastic Puzzle" - Unknown Author
>>

I am sorting through the list of Arcadian and Cursor programs, checking what has been and has not been archived on BallyAlley.com.  I discovered the author and true name of the "Plastic Puzzle" program that Paul archived in 300-baud format.

Thanks for describing the program, Paul.  When I was leafing through the pages of Cursor this morning, it was Paul's description that made the game's name "click" with me (when I read Fred Cornett saying that the game utilizes his previously published Plastic Puzzle program).  This isn't an unknown program-- it was actually published in a newsletter.  Here is more information about it:

Rotate
by Robert Leake
Cursor 1, no. 3 (March 1980): 22-23.

This program utilizes the Plastic Puzzle (CURSOR Feb 80) concept and moves it light years in complexity.

This program was found on a hand-labeled tape in Ken Lill's tape collection which was otherwise filled with programs from The Arcadian and Cursor. Originally, Paul Thacker had been unable to match it up with any known programs-- thus, without a proper name to attribute to he program, it was archived as "Plastic Puzzle." Now the program has been identified and the name is corrected in the archive.

The newsletter has full documentation for this game, as well has a full program explanation.  You can download Rotate for Bally BASIC, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#RotateBB

For those with a Bally BASIC interface, give the game a try.  For those without it-- well, then load it via the 300-to-2000 conversion program.

14426:
I've got too many projects half-way finished. I'm going to go ahead and finish up and upload any programs I've got archived. Then I can think about what I might archive next. So, here's a grab bag of various software, uploaded to the FTP server for Adam to add to the website when he gets a chance.

AstroBASIC:

Hand Control Test (1982)(New Image)(2000 baud)(PD)[a] - found in Bob Fabris collection on hand-labeled tape from New Image that says "Freebies". It has a simpler title screen than the previously archived version.


Bally BASIC:

Logo (for Starship and Can You Quit) (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)(proto),
Starship (19xx)(Ken Lill)(2000 baud)(proto)[a2],
Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)(proto),
Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)(proto)[a] - all of these were found on a tape in Ken Lill's collection hand-labeled “At  0 @357=Logo, At 100 @257=STREAP, At 160 @258=Can You Quit”. I'm not sure if I read the number 357 correctly. The following four programs were on a single side of the tape.
1) A logo screen that says this is Tape #1 from Gambits, and that Side 1 contains “Starship!” and Side 2 contains “Can You Quit?”.
2) A version of Starship that controls a little differently than the previously archived versions. Push the joystick left and pull the trigger to use guns, and push it right and pull the trigger to use bombs. It also seems unfinished. Once your ammo is depleted, there seems to be nothing to do other than wait to be destroyed.
3)  A version of “Can You Quit?” that draws a diamond-shaped board, rolls some dice, and then appears to freeze up. I'd actually seen a version of this before, but hadn't been able to identify it. I had named it “ZZZ-UNK-Dice (19xx)(possibly Karl Nystrom)(300 baud)”, but will now suggest it be named “Can You Quit (19xx)(Ken Lill)(300 baud)”. I never figured out the rules to the game, but the previously archived one at least seems playable.
4) Another version of “Can You Quit?”. It looks very similar to the previous load, but now there's a line moving over some of the dice. I still couldn't find a way to interact with it, though.
So far as I'm aware, none of these programs were ever released for sale.

Bangman (19xx)(Ernie Sams)(h -)(300 baud) – archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection hand-labeled “Bangman, Backgammon”, with the reverse side hand-labeled “New Checkers, Maze Services”. It has several code changes as compared to any version of Bangman I've seen before. I don't know for sure who made the modifications.

Backgammon (19xx)(-)(300 baud)(proto) - archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection hand-labeled “Bangman, Backgammon”, with the reverse side hand-labeled “New Checkers, Maze Services”. It only draws the board.

ZZZ-UNK-Pattern-Width (19xx)(-)(300 baud)[b] - archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection hand-labeled “Bangman, Backgammon”, with the reverse side hand-labeled “New Checkers, Maze Services”. The beginning of the program was missing on the tape. In the extant code, the first thing it does is ask for a pattern width. Other text includes “CRASH”, “WRONG” and “SCORE = ”. As is, it crashes immediately. If anyone recognizes this program, please let me know.

Welcome To My Office (19xx)(-)(300 baud)(proto) - archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection hand-labeled “Bangman, Backgammon”, with the reverse side hand-labeled “New Checkers, Maze Services”. It simulates a visit to a doctor (probably a psychologist, reminiscent of programs like Eliza or New Image's Sick-o Therapy), but doesn't get past the introductions.

ZZZ-UNK-List-Code (19xx)(-)(300 baud)(proto) - archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection hand-labeled “Bangman, Backgammon”, with the reverse side hand-labeled “New Checkers, Maze Services”. All it actually does is list its own code, followed by printing a bunch of question marks. I assume its unfinished, but I'm not sure what purpose was intended.

Checkers (19xx)(John Collins)(h -)(300 baud) – archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection hand-labeled “New Checkers, Maze Services”, with the reverse side hand-labeled “Bangman, Backgammon”. It has several code changes as compared to the John Collins checkers programs printed in The Arcadian. It seems closer to the first program than to Checkers II and later updates.

Maze Services (19xx)(-)(300 baud) - archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection hand-labeled “New Checkers, Maze Services”, with the reverse side hand-labeled “Bangman, Backgammon”. It only draws a maze with no entrance and exit.


RAM Expansion:

Blue Ram Utility (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud) – archived from tape of many RAM expansion programs compiled by Mike White. Queue up both loads, enter “:INPUT; RUN” into AstroBASIC, and play.

Blue Ram Utility (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud)[a] – archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection. The tape has the official Perkins Engineering Blue Ram label, but the only identification of the program is a hand-written “Utility”. Queue up both loads, enter “:INPUT; RUN” into AstroBASIC, and play. The code differs slightly from Blue Ram Utility (1982)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud). The tape has AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of the Blue Ram Utility on one side, and AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of Blue Ram Diagnostic on the other. 

Blue Ram Diagnostic (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(proto) – archived from tape in Bob Fabris's collection hand-labeled simply “Blue Ram Diagnostic”. Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. It differs from the previously archived Blue Ram Diagnostic dated 6-2-80. I found that version in both Bob Fabris's and Ken Lill's collections. On one tape, it was labeled as version 1.0. This version has no date and no machine language portion, so I believe it is likely an earlier prototype.

Music Compiler (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(proto) – found in Ken Lill's collection on a tape hand-labeled “Music Compiler”. The other side contained Sarabande. I believe this should be loaded into Bally BASIC with :INPUT, followed by loading music data with :INPUT.

The first mention of this program is in Arcadian volume 2, issue 10, page 97, in which Perkins Engineering describes upcoming software for use with the Blue Ram expansion:

"Then we will provide the software necessary to have the Blue Ram act as a compiler for music programs. Using Processor Technology format, one can simply enter musical selections and the software will convert that into the proper language that the Bally can understand."

The next mention comes in Arcadian volume 3, issue 2, page 18. The news here talks about John Perkins giving a demonstration of the Blue Ram to a computer club:

"Next, we listened with pleasure to several Bally compiled musical selections from Bach and Handel in three part harmony. It was explained that the compiler is used to translate a person's own composition or regular sheet music into a form that is played by the Bally."

And that's actually the last I can find. The fact that it's never actually advertised makes me think that it was never released, although it clearly got to a point where it was usable.

The only music I found for this is Sarabande. Handel composed a song named Sarabande, so this fits with the newsletter. Unfortunately, the versions of Sarabande and Music Compiler seem to be incompatible. For example, they even use a different address range for storing the music data. I got some suggestions from Richard Degler, but even after cleaning up the Sarabande code and changing the address range, I still couldn't get Music Compiler to play music. If anyone figures out how to get this working, let us know.

Sarabande (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(Music Compiler)(proto) – for general information, see the Music Compiler description. This was found in Ken Lill's collection on a tape hand-labeled “Music - Sarabande”. The other side contained Music Compiler. I believe this should be loaded into Bally BASIC with :INPUT after loading Music Compiler. Sarabande is a little strange because there
are actually two sections on the tape, the second one much shorter and lower volume. The first section ends with U&(64)=0. The second has a few bytes not seen in the first section, then U&(64)=0
again, then a STOP TAPE message followed by :RETURN; RUN. My best guess was that the extra bytes and U&(64)=0 in the second part should be removed, but even doing this, and changing the address range to that used in Music Compiler, I still didn't manage to play a song. Therefore, I am uploading this exactly as I found it on the tape. If anyone figures out how to get this working, let us know. 

Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud) – archived from tape in Bob Fabris's collection hand-labeled “Blue Ram Utility 1.0 Copy”. Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. The code matches a printout found in Bob Fabris's documents.

Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)[a] – archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection . The tape has the official Perkins Engineering Blue Ram label, but the only identification of the program is a hand-written “Utility”. Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. The BASIC code is identical to Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud), while the machine code portion differs slightly. Both versions seemed to process correctly, and to run alright. The tape has AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of the Blue Ram Utility on one side, and AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of Blue Ram Diagnostic on the other.

Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(proto) - found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "BR UTIL". Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. As compared to the version I believe was the released one, it is missing the machine language portion. The BASIC code has several differences as compared to the other archived versions.

Blue Ram Utility (1980)(Perkins Engineering)(300 baud)(proto)[a] – found in Bob Fabris's tape collection on tape hand-labeled “Blue Ram Utility”. Load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. As compared to the version I believe was the released one, it is missing the machine language portion. The BASIC code has several differences as compared to the other archived versions.

Blue Ram Diagnostic (198x)(Perkins Engineering)(2000 baud) - archived from tape in Ken Lill's collection.  The tape has the official Perkins Engineering Blue Ram label, but the only identification of the program is a hand-written “Diagnostic”. The tape has AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of the Blue Ram Utility on one side, and AstroBASIC and Bally BASIC versions of Blue Ram Diagnostic on the other. The tape label gives these loading instructions:

Astro INPUT; RUN Mode = RAM (Center)

There are two loads, the second one very short. I found this a little confusing, as the program started once the first load was finished, even if I only loaded it with :INPUT, not using RUN. The first line of the program does have a conditional :INPUT %(28672), so perhaps the second load would be used in specific circumstances. The test is IF A=0.

Paul

I've seen some WaveMakers tapes organized like this:
short 300 baud introduction programentire 2000 baud programmain 300 baud program
So the 2000 baud program was actually put into a break in the 300 baud program. While the 300 baud intro animation was running, the recorder would be playing the 2000 baud program, which Bally BASIC would simply ignore. Once the animation was finished, more 300 baud data would be ready to go. It's certainly space efficient, though a little annoying for me.
Paul

14433:
Hi everyone!
 

 My name is Nathan. I started fooling around with Astrocade programming about three weeks ago, and I've enjoyed trawling through all of the documentation online. I've gotten some rudimentary programs running so far (menus, rectangles, colors, etc.) and I'm now working on drawing patterns. I hadn't heard of the Astrocade until recently, and I'm fascinated with what it can do.
 

 Anyhow, one frustration with programming (beyond switching my brain from 6502 assembly and the NES architecture) is the sometimes cryptic organization of the Nutting Manual and the diaspora of tutorials and FAQs that exist online. Bouncing between these different resources was impeding doing actual work on the machine.
 

 So, in an effort to give back to the Astrocade community (and perhaps entice new folks to explore), I've put together a resource called the Better Bally Book http://metopal.com/projects/ballybook/, which is a wiki-style 'rewrite' of the Nutting Manual. I wanted to get all the known programming information into a single, searchable, and editable database that people could easily update. 
 

 I started this weekend, and I already have a good amount done. There are still a few dozen system routines to transcribe and lots of external documentation to integrate, but the main framework is there. I've made some organizational decisions that change the Nutting Manual's original layout, but they're all in an effort to make learning simpler and more logical. And the wiki makes it so much easier to jump around than paging through the Nutting Manual PDF.
 

 I hope you'll all take a few moments to look around and offer feedback. Right now, wiki registration is limited to myself while I get the basic framework done, but if the community was interested, I could open registration.
 

 Nathan
14434:
Wow, Nathan has really dug into the Bally system!  It's great to see someone "discover" this system for the first time.  I took a look at the wiki site for the Better Bally Book (Nathan, you did all that in a weekend?!?), and it's looking good (from what I've browsed through so far).  I have a few questions/comments:


1) I suppose that you're grabbing the text from the "Nutting Manual" from the retyped version, rather than OCRing the manual, right?


2) You mention that you'll be "eliminating irrelevant information (e.g., the high-resolution mode)."  Why eliminate references to high-res mode (also known as commercial mode)?  The "Nutting manual" is meant to show a programmer how to program the Bally Professional Arcade and the Bally arcade high-res hardware (i.e. Seawolf II, Extra Bases, Space Zap, Wizard of Wor, Gorf, and The Adventures of Robby Roto).  Also, the Bally Arcade can technically be upgraded to hi-res (with difficulty-- I know of no users who have done this since the 80s).  Because of this, keeping the references to hi-res mode seems required.  Finally, perhaps the most important reason to keep references to the hi-res mode in the Better Bally Book is that the Bally Arcade's 8K ROM does actually have to set the system to low-res mode upon startup.  It does this at location $0003 of the system ROM:


OUT     (CONCM),A       ; *** SET CONSUMER MODE ***


CONCM is referenced in the Bally header file:


CONCM   EQU     $08     ; &(8)= ; write 0 for CONsumer, 1 for CoMmercial mode


3)  Andy Guevara's series of articles called The Bit Fiddler's Corner, published in the Arcadian in 1983 and 1984, were extremely helpful to me when I was first learning about the Bally.  Maybe you can link to the compilation that I made of the series:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Bit%20Fiddler/Bit%20Fiddler's%20Corner%20%281983%29%28Andy%20Guevara%29.pdf


4) I like that you're going to provide a glossary.


5) Do you have a real Astrocade, or are you working under emulation?


6) The Nutting Manual++, a project that never really got off the ground, has just one addition relating the the DISNUM routine (on page 34 of the manual).  I'm not sure if you want to include that in the BBB.


7) I guess it's time that I update the homebrew area of BallyAlley.com.  Several of those programs will not work under current versions of the Astrocade emulator in MAME (or on real hardware) because the interrupt mode is set wrong.  Early versions of MESS used to not care.  For the broken programs, the Interrupt Mode must be changed from $18 to $08 (screen interrupts only).


8) I've not worked on a wiki page before.  I gave up on even trying that that years ago after any changes I made to the Astrocade page on Wikipedia kept getting reverted back to the previous version.  However, Nathan, if you need help, then I'd surely be willing to contribute whatever I can to this worthy project!


9) My guess is that the Better Bally Book is a means toward an end, and not an end to itself.  Nathan, what are your plans for playing around with the Bally hardware?


This Better Bally Book has been a great, quite pleasant, surprise!


Adam
