14435:
Hey Adam 

 Glad it's a pleasant surprise! The BBB has been a bit of an obsession for the past few days, and I'm excited for what it can become.
 

 As for your questions:
 

 1) I'm looking at the version on archive.org and retyping by hand. This is giving me the chance to absorb and learn the information while I read and type. Reading the NM multiple times through has been really beneficial to my understanding.
 

 2) I've thought quite a bit about this. I understand what you mean about including hi-rez mode, but practically, how many people are going to program for *arcade* hardware (or a difficult console mod) vs. the Astrocade? I'd guess zero or close to it. I'm aware of the need to set consumer mode and note that multiple times, and I specifically mention commercial mode with reference to the original manual. The BBB doesn't erase the NM, so someone could still seek that info out. But I think for a beginner, it might be confusing? I've taken the same view on Rotate, which I mention, but don't spend time explaining or illustrating it. But I don't know, there could always be a small 'arcade' section of BBB with all the cut parts.
 

 3) I've looked at a few, but yeah, I'll link it up and dive a bit deeper to see what's useful. Thanks!
 

 4) Glossaries are crucial! Definitely didn't know what a DOPE vector was before this weekend...
 

 5) I don't own an Astrocade yet. I've been perusing eBay, but the prices are silly, so I'm waiting for a lucky break. Emulation is an unfortunate necessity. Being on a Mac and having to switch to Windows to test things out is a drag too. I tried for a whole day to get a Mac workflow going, but I couldn't get zmac to compile properly. Maybe someone more versed in that kind of thing could figure it out for me.
 

 6) I'll check it out, thanks.
 

 7) That'd be awesome.
 

 8) The Wiki software isn't too bad once you get the hang of it, but if you just want to pass along suggestions or content, that'd be great too. I'll add as much as I can. I have LOTS of technical questions that I'll be bugging everyone with. Some of the NM sections are really opaque, and I'd like to rewrite them with much better clarity.
 

 9) Lots of plans. First, I got interested in the project due to frustration with trying to piece together documentation in a sensible manner. You really need to jump around in the NM, and without a print copy, that was a chore. I'm fascinated with the Astrocade because it's a really interesting machine. Really it was the horizontal color boundary that sold me. What a weird, interesting technical feature! I love platforms with character, and I'm really interested, as a games scholar, in platforms that 'lost,' especially when they were technically superior. I mean, Astrocade is worlds better than Atari VCS, but the latter 'won' for a variety of reasons. That's interesting. Likewise for the hobbyist/BASIC community that grew around the machine after its commercial demise.
 

 So I'm considering a writing project involving the Astrocade. (I already wrote a book about the NES called I AM ERROR that has a similar spirit to what I'm thinking about.) Anyhow, the BBB is part of the technical research necessary to make that project real.
 

 I also want to make some games! I have a notebook of ideas I'd like to try out once I've spent some time grappling with learning and programming the Z80. I find the Astrocade really intuitive (especially compared to the NES), so it's been a lot of fun. I have some odd artsy stuff I'd like to try out too. :) We'll see what happens. No promises. But if anything, I'll leave behind the BBB for other new explorers to use.
 

 N
14436:
I found the Blue RAM Utility ( upgraded to the RWB Utility on the UltiMulti carts version 2 and above) to be extremely helpful to me when I was learning Z-80 machine language. It requires Blue RAM BASIC and an extended memory on an original unit. I don't do MESS so I don't know if it is emulated. It has an on-the-fly dis-assembler and a pretty good editor. You can also test your program through it. There are many non-usable parts to it (especially BRU) like 300 BAUD modem programs. Michael Garber and Richard Degler are 2 absolutely GREAT programmers for the Bally / Astrocade. Brett Bilbrey is also good, but has been away for some time (about 30 years).I use the DN manual quite often myself. If I can be of any assistance, please let me know.
Ken Lill

 Subject: [ballyalley] Re: The Better Bally Book

    Hey Adam
Glad it's a pleasant surprise! The BBB has been a bit of an obsession for the past few days, and I'm excited for what it can become.
As for your questions:
1) I'm looking at the version on archive.org and retyping by hand. This is giving me the chance to absorb and learn the information while I read and type. Reading the NM multiple times through has been really beneficial to my understanding.
2) I've thought quite a bit about this. I understand what you mean about including hi-rez mode, but practically, how many people are going to program for *arcade* hardware (or a difficult console mod) vs. the Astrocade? I'd guess zero or close to it. I'm aware of the need to set consumer mode and note that multiple times, and I specifically mention commercial mode with reference to the original manual. The BBB doesn't erase the NM, so someone could still seek that info out. But I think for a beginner, it might be confusing? I've taken the same view on Rotate, which I mention, but don't spend time explaining or illustrating it. But I don't know, there could always be a small 'arcade' section of BBB with all the cut parts.
3) I've looked at a few, but yeah, I'll link it up and dive a bit deeper to see what's useful. Thanks!
4) Glossaries are crucial! Definitely didn't know what a DOPE vector was before this weekend...
5) I don't own an Astrocade yet. I've been perusing eBay, but the prices are silly, so I'm waiting for a lucky break. Emulation is an unfortunate necessity. Being on a Mac and having to switch to Windows to test things out is a drag too. I tried for a whole day to get a Mac workflow going, but I couldn't get zmac to compile properly. Maybe someone more versed in that kind of thing could figure it out for me.
6) I'll check it out, thanks.
7) That'd be awesome.
8) The Wiki software isn't too bad once you get the hang of it, but if you just want to pass along suggestions or content, that'd be great too. I'll add as much as I can. I have LOTS of technical questions that I'll be bugging everyone with. Some of the NM sections are really opaque, and I'd like to rewrite them with much better clarity.
9) Lots of plans. First, I got interested in the project due to frustration with trying to piece together documentation in a sensible manner. You really need to jump around in the NM, and without a print copy, that was a chore. I'm fascinated with the Astrocade because it's a really interesting machine. Really it was the horizontal color boundary that sold me. What a weird, interesting technical feature! I love platforms with character, and I'm really interested, as a games scholar, in platforms that 'lost,' especially when they were technically superior. I mean, Astrocade is worlds better than Atari VCS, but the latter 'won' for a variety of reasons. That's interesting. Likewise for the hobbyist/BASIC community that grew around the machine after its commercial demise.
So I'm considering a writing project involving the Astrocade. (I already wrote a book about the NES called I AM ERROR that has a similar spirit to what I'm thinking about.) Anyhow, the BBB is part of the technical research necessary to make that project real.
I also want to make some games! I have a notebook of ideas I'd like to try out once I've spent some time grappling with learning and programming the Z80. I find the Astrocade really intuitive (especially compared to the NES), so it's been a lot of fun. I have some odd artsy stuff I'd like to try out too. :) We'll see what happens. No promises. But if anything, I'll leave behind the BBB for other new explorers to use.

I have been looking at the code every Friday and/or Saturday. However, I haven't been posting regularly as I should.

I was going to argue against posting on AtariAge just yet, partly to hide my ignorance. I may re-consider...

There is still so much I don't know about this code.

I still haven't found the maze making routines yet.

I did decipher what five of the six User System Routines do:


#1 Routine checks from Table below While decrementing C
   Set A Between 121 & 1. Anything over 121 will be A=120 C=10
   Returns A=Closest lesser value. C=count 10-0.
   IF A is over 121 Returns A=120 C=10
		
      $78 - 120
      $6C - 108
      $60 - 96
      $54 - 84
      $48 - 72
      $3C - 60
      $30 - 48
      $24 - 36
      $18 - 24
      $0C - 12
      $00 - 0

#2 Set A to first value and B to second value
   Calls #1, Loads A with B and B with C
   Calls #1, Loads A with B Subtracts C
   Returns A = C1-C2
   That is Table index one minus Table index two.
   Actual Table values tossed.

#3 Set IX to Block B
   Blocks start at 4E6C and are 31 Bytes apart.

#5 Load HL from (IY+4)(IY+5), Load DE from (IX+4)(IX+5)

#6 Load DE from (IX+4)(IX+5)

I haven't come up with names or header blocks for them yet.

#4 is quite long and has calls to other parts of the code...

I did find the sprite draw routines. Labelled those.

In the code above it I found a really cool trick!

We know the MAGIC register uses bits 0-6. Bit 6 (64) being FLOP (Draw pixels right to left).

Well, The Wizard uses bit 7 (128) in its vector block MAGIC slot! It is used as the FLIP bit! (Like I was using Flipping and FLOPping on my skeleton demo)

The hardware totally ignores it. The code above the sprite draw routines picks it up and assigns a negative value causing the draw to happen bottom up rather than top down.

I was a bit annoyed that I should have realized I could have done the same in my demo, but quite surprised with the use if the 7th bit as a pseudo-MAGIC function.

I'm under the impression that the code I'm looking at was the result of Bally's Turse(?) programming language being compiled down to Z80. It could just be me though.

Another mystery, similar to the last is between L3399: and a little below L33BB: is a block of code I've labelled as Pointless...

It uses GAMme DIFficulty and (IX+7) of a Vblock? to determine what value to get from the table at L33E3. All fine and good, but instead of using that value, we immediately replace it with (IX+2) and continue on...

I'm attaching my working copy, as I'm sure I've forgotten to mention something I marked in there and I've changed some hard coded addresses to working labels.

On 16-05-26 10:41 PM, John Mezzacappa jjpm74@yahoo.com [ballyalley] wrote:
>
> Not to stray too far, a few of my old lists were asking for a Bally Home
> Computer. This was in 1979 and 1980. Was this the same thing as the
> Astrocade/Videocade, or did Bally offer another system during this time?
>
> Cheers,

> John
>

It was originally released for sale through mail order in 1977 as the Bally Home Library Computer. In 1978 it was released to a wider market as the Bally Professional Arcade.

Pictures of a white unit with Bally Computer system atop a keyboard expansion circulated around that time.

Later Bally did release a limited amount of white units and many more regular units with the Bally Computer system label.

At that time Astrovision bought the home division from Bally and continued to sell for a limited time mostly Bally Computer system labelled units. Some Professional arcade labels may be found in their boxes too.

After an aborted attempt to change the label to Astro Professional Arcade, Astrovision changed both it's name and the system to Astrocade.

Page of scans here:

http://www.glankonian.com/~lance/Unit%20Labels.html

#4 is quite long and has calls to other parts of the code...

I did find the sprite draw routines. Labelled those.

In the code above it I found a really cool trick!

We know the MAGIC register uses bits 0-6. Bit 6 (64) being FLOP (Draw
pixels right to left).

Well, The Wizard uses bit 7 (128) in its vector block MAGIC slot! It is
used as the FLIP bit! (Like I was using Flipping and FLOPping on my
skeleton demo)

The hardware totally ignores it. The code above the sprite draw routines
picks it up and assigns a negative value causing the draw to happen
bottom up rather than top down.

I was a bit annoyed that I should have realized I could have done the
same in my demo, but quite surprised with the use if the 7th bit as a
pseudo-MAGIC function.

I'm under the impression that the code I'm looking at was the result of
Bally's Turse(?) programming language being compiled down to Z80. It
could just be me though.

Another mystery, similar to the last is between L3399: and a little
below L33BB: is a block of code I've labelled as Pointless...

It uses GAMme DIFficulty and (IX+7) of a Vblock? to determine what value
to get from the table at L33E3. All fine and good, but instead of using
that value, we immediately replace it with (IX+2) and continue on...

I'm attaching my working copy, as I'm sure I've forgotten to mention
something I marked in there and I've changed some hard coded addresses
to working labels.

You can also test your program through it. There are many non-usable parts to it (especially BRU) like 300 BAUD modem programs. Michael Garber and Richard Degler are 2 absolutely GREAT programmers for the Bally / Astrocade. Ken Lill

    Hey Adam
Glad it's a pleasant surprise! The BBB has been a bit of an obsession for the past few days, and I'm excited for what it can become.
As for your questions:
1) I'm looking at the version on archive.org and retyping by hand. This is giving me the chance to absorb and learn the information while I read and type. Reading the NM multiple times through has been really beneficial to my understanding.
2) I've thought quite a bit about this. I understand what you mean about including hi-rez mode, but practically, how many people are going to program for *arcade* hardware (or a difficult console mod) vs. the Astrocade? I'd guess zero or close to it. I'm aware of the need to set consumer mode and note that multiple times, and I specifically mention commercial mode with reference to the original manual. The BBB doesn't erase the NM, so someone could still seek that info out. But I think for a beginner, it might be confusing? I've taken the same view on Rotate, which I mention, but don't spend time explaining or illustrating it. But I don't know, there could always be a small 'arcade' section of BBB with all the cut parts.
3) I've looked at a few, but yeah, I'll link it up and dive a bit deeper to see what's useful. Thanks!
4) Glossaries are crucial! Definitely didn't know what a DOPE vector was before this weekend...
5) I don't own an Astrocade yet. I've been perusing eBay, but the prices are silly, so I'm waiting for a lucky break. Emulation is an unfortunate necessity. Being on a Mac and having to switch to Windows to test things out is a drag too. I tried for a whole day to get a Mac workflow going, but I couldn't get zmac to compile properly. Maybe someone more versed in that kind of thing could figure it out for me.
6) I'll check it out, thanks.
7) That'd be awesome.
8) The Wiki software isn't too bad once you get the hang of it, but if you just want to pass along suggestions or content, that'd be great too. I'll add as much as I can. I have LOTS of technical questions that I'll be bugging everyone with. Some of the NM sections are really opaque, and I'd like to rewrite them with much better clarity.
9) Lots of plans. First, I got interested in the project due to frustration with trying to piece together documentation in a sensible manner. You really need to jump around in the NM, and without a print copy, that was a chore. I'm fascinated with the Astrocade because it's a really interesting machine. Really it was the horizontal color boundary that sold me. What a weird, interesting technical feature! I love platforms with character, and I'm really interested, as a games scholar, in platforms that 'lost,' especially when they were technically superior. I mean, Astrocade is worlds better than Atari VCS, but the latter 'won' for a variety of reasons. That's interesting. Likewise for the hobbyist/BASIC community that grew around the machine after its commercial demise.
So I'm considering a writing project involving the Astrocade. (I already wrote a book about the NES called I AM ERROR that has a similar spirit to what I'm thinking about.) Anyhow, the BBB is part of the technical research necessary to make that project real.
I also want to make some games! I have a notebook of ideas I'd like to try out once I've spent some time grappling with learning and programming the Z80. I find the Astrocade really intuitive (especially compared to the NES), so it's been a lot of fun. I have some odd artsy stuff I'd like to try out too. :) We'll see what happens. No promises. But if anything, I'll leave behind the BBB for other new explorers to use.
N

I found the Blue RAM Utility ( upgraded to the RWB Utility on the UltiMulti carts version 2 and above) to be extremely helpful to me when I was learning Z-80 machine language. It requires Blue RAM BASIC and an extended memory on an original unit. I don't do MESS so I don't know if it is emulated. It has an on-the-fly dis-assembler and a pretty good editor. You can also test your program through it. There are many non-usable parts to it (especially BRU) like 300 BAUD modem programs. Michael Garber and Richard Degler are 2 absolutely GREAT programmers for the Bally / Astrocade. Brett Bilbrey is also good, but has been away for some time (about 30 years).
I use the DN manual quite often myself. If I can be of any assistance, please let me know.

Ken Lill

Subject: [ballyalley] Re: The Better Bally Book


Hey Adam

Glad it's a pleasant surprise! The BBB has been a bit of an obsession for the past few days, and I'm excited for what it can become.

As for your questions:

1) I'm looking at the version on archive.org and retyping by hand. This is giving me the chance to absorb and learn the information while I read and type. Reading the NM multiple times through has been really beneficial to my understanding.

2) I've thought quite a bit about this. I understand what you mean about including hi-rez mode, but practically, how many people are going to program for *arcade* hardware (or a difficult console mod) vs. the Astrocade? I'd guess zero or close to it. I'm aware of the need to set consumer mode and note that multiple times, and I specifically mention commercial mode with reference to the original manual. The BBB doesn't erase the NM, so someone could still seek that info out. But I think for a beginner, it might be confusing? I've taken the same view on Rotate, which I mention, but don't spend time explaining or illustrating it. But I don't know, there could always be a small 'arcade' section of BBB with all the cut parts.

3) I've looked at a few, but yeah, I'll link it up and dive a bit deeper to see what's useful. Thanks!

4) Glossaries are crucial! Definitely didn't know what a DOPE vector was before this weekend...

5) I don't own an Astrocade yet. I've been perusing eBay, but the prices are silly, so I'm waiting for a lucky break. Emulation is an unfortunate necessity. Being on a Mac and having to switch to Windows to test things out is a drag too. I tried for a whole day to get a Mac workflow going, but I couldn't get zmac to compile properly. Maybe someone more versed in that kind of thing could figure it out for me.

6) I'll check it out, thanks.

7) That'd be awesome.

8) The Wiki software isn't too bad once you get the hang of it, but if you just want to pass along suggestions or content, that'd be great too. I'll add as much as I can. I have LOTS of technical questions that I'll be bugging everyone with. Some of the NM sections are really opaque, and I'd like to rewrite them with much better clarity.

9) Lots of plans. First, I got interested in the project due to frustration with trying to piece together documentation in a sensible manner. You really need to jump around in the NM, and without a print copy, that was a chore. I'm fascinated with the Astrocade because it's a really interesting machine. Really it was the horizontal color boundary that sold me. What a weird, interesting technical feature! I love platforms with character, and I'm really interested, as a games scholar, in platforms that 'lost,' especially when they were technically superior. I mean, Astrocade is worlds better than Atari VCS, but the latter 'won' for a variety of reasons. That's interesting. Likewise for the hobbyist/BASIC community that grew around the machine after its commercial demise.

So I'm considering a writing project involving the Astrocade. (I already wrote a book about the NES called I AM ERROR that has a similar spirit to what I'm thinking about.) Anyhow, the BBB is part of the technical research necessary to make that project real.

I also want to make some games! I have a notebook of ideas I'd like to try out once I've spent some time grappling with learning and programming the Z80. I find the Astrocade really intuitive (especially compared to the NES), so it's been a lot of fun. I have some odd artsy stuff I'd like to try out too. :) We'll see what happens. No promises. But if anything, I'll leave behind the BBB for other new explorers to use.

N

Maybe someone more versed in that kind of thing could figure it out for me.

6) I'll check it out, thanks.

Really it was the horizontal color boundary that sold me. What a weird, interesting technical feature! I love platforms with character, and I'm really interested, as a games scholar, in platforms that 'lost,' especially when they were technically superior. I mean, Astrocade is worlds better than Atari VCS, but the latter 'won' for a variety of reasons. That's interesting. Likewise for the hobbyist/BASIC community that grew around the machine after its commercial demise.

I also want to make some games! I have a notebook of ideas I'd like to try out once I've spent some time grappling with learning and programming the Z80. I find the Astrocade really intuitive (especially compared to the NES), so it's been a lot of fun. I have some odd artsy stuff I'd like to try out too. :) We'll see what happens. No promises. But if anything, I'll leave behind the BBB for other new explorers to use.

N

Treasure Cove is the main game for Round 8 of the Astrocade High Score Club. The bonus game is Castle of Horror. "Treasure Cove requires your scuba diver to descend to the sea floor and bring treasures back to your diving boat, slowly circling above, before his air runs out. Simple enough, except for the killer fish, squid, crab, etc., that roam about - and the ever present octopus that guards the treasure! As you clear each treasure-laden area, you move to a new spot, with more valuable treasures - and more denizens of the deep. Twenty screens in all. Tournament Level for uniform competitive play with up to four players. Features continuous music."

Here is an overview of Castle of Horror:

"You will find yourself in a castle. Surrounded by monsters whose only mission is to kill and destroy. You are the target. Your only defense is to build a barricade around yourself before the monsters can get to you. The monsters will die if they hit your wall, however some monsters have more power than others and can destroy your barricade, allowing remaining monsters to pass through. You must destroy all monsters in the room to go on to your next challenge. As game progresses more monsters enter the battle.

"This game has all the quality of a cartridge and the challenge of an arcade. Uses one joystick, machine graphics, and excellent sound. Side two contains Four Famous Freebees. This cassette is in Astro-BASIC only."

14464:
I'm afraid so. Blue RAM BASIC Programs have 3 different spaces that they need to access. The 1st is the !6000 - !6C1E area of RAM. When Blue RAM BASIC does a cold start, then it completely clears this area. The next area it can load to is !7000 - !FFFF. However there was never a Blue RAM unit with RAM that high.The last place be loaded usually was !6C20 - just before the stack area. These are all of the variables in the Memory Allocation Table. You CAN'T just do one load. It will crash the stack and you will lose it all, including Blue RAM BASIC. The other problem is the warm boot needed. you will have to jump to it to prevent BRB from clearing the !6000 area. This would take someone like Richard Degler or Michael Garber to fix it for the aptly named program, MESS.Ken

14468:
I got a VIPER expansion when Adam and I acquired Bob Fabris's collection. I don't think I've used it since I got the Lil' White RAM, or at least not much. The Lil' White is more compact, and the VIPER can't run any additional programs.

We went into a lot of detail about RAM expansions in the Yahoo group when I was adding RAM expansion support to MESS. The VIPER's 16K memory is mapped from $6000 to $9FFF. As far as I know, the switches on the various expansions all work the same, aside from the massively configurable R&L board. A RAM protect switch can be flipped at any time to make the RAM act like ROM. They also have a range switch.  The default position is 6K, but it can be switched to 2K.  This means that the expanded memory starting at $6000 will instead be mapped to the cartridge memory starting at $2000.
I don't really remember about VIPERSoft BASIC, but Ken noted in a message from June 7, 2010, "Vipersoft and Hot Rod Bally BASIC will NOT run on a 4K Blue RAM because they reside starting at $7000".
Paul

On February 17, 2010 (in message #8535), Paul Thacker wrote:
>>
I've located some Arcadian ads in Kilobaud through Google book search, but they only display snippet view. They're in 1978 page 120, and 1979 page 128.
>>

I rediscovered this 6-year-old post today while doing some research into the early issues of the Arcadian for episode #2 of the Bally Alley Astrocast podcast.  The Arcadians (the pre-Arcadian) newsletter #4 (September  1978) alludes to this original classified ad for the Arcadian newsletter.  I found it by methodically going through entire issues of Kilobaud magazine archived on archive.org.  The classified ad appeared in Kilobaud, no. 21 (Sept. 1978): 120.  The ad is in the first column, and it is the tenth one from the top.  It's simple, short and to the point when it announces:

"Bally Owners and hopefuls are banding together for our mutual benefit to extract the maximum usefulness from this unit.  Anyone interested is invited to write Bob Fabris, 3626 Morrie Dr., San Jose CA 95127 with a SASE"

With that brief note, Mr. Fabris started a Bally tradition that still is being felt among Bally owners and users to this day.  You can see the (quite tiny) ad here:

https://archive.org/stream/kilobaudmagazine-1978-09/Kilobaud_1978_September#page/n120/mode/1up

I'm currently downloading the September 1978 issue of Kilobaud.  It's quite large (6.2GB).  When I'm done, I'm going to extract the cover page and classified ads and place them onto BallyAlley.com.

Adam

Since I'm off to vacation for a few days, I thought I'd post an update on the BBB. Most every bit of the NM is now transferred (except for the technical/electrical info near the end). Indeed, transferred, heavily revised and annotated. I'm really pleased with how the documentation is turning out, as I've been using it every day while I experiment around with Arcade programming.
 

 Major segments have been rewritten or updated. The interrupts http://metopal.com/projects/ballybook/doku.php?id=hardware:interrupts section now has far more description (and examples) of how screen interrupts function. I still don't fully grasp their practical use, but it's a good start (and they work in testing). I'm particularly proud of the alphanumeric display http://metopal.com/projects/ballybook/doku.php?id=software:alphanumeric section. I spent a lot of time probing the system routines and figuring out how text is rendered. I put copious pictures, examples, an additional documentation there as well. Didn't understand ASCII control codes before? BBB has you covered.
 

 Lots of tiny details too, like renaming sections and reorganizing content (e.g., Object Vectors instead of Screen Vectoring Routines) to clarify programming techniques. There are code snippets and a glossary too.
 

 But I still have a ton to learn, and I could use some help on some technical details. Here's a few (well, a lot):
 

 * I could really use some documentation for the BCD math routines. Their documentation is sparse, and I don't quite grok BCD math enough to write them on my own.
 

 * What is a 'SACRED register load'? This terminology is referenced in the SUCK and INDEXB routines, but I can't find clarification.
 

 * I think I get RELABS, but I'm not sure I understand its distinction from RELAB1.
 

 * MSKTD is fairly mysterious as well. Any clarification on that routine would be helpful (beyond the 'Vector animation' tutorial, I mean), especially practical usage.
 

 * I haven't tackled expansion hardware at all. What's a good resource? What software used it and how?
 

 * Interrupt scheduling. How is it managed, say for changed palette values as the screen is drawn? How did games use interrupts for timing? 
 

 * Limitations. How many patterns can be drawn or vectored per frame / screen? How much does it take to bog down the Arcade?
 

 * Light pens. Were these commercially released? Used in software? Is there any extant documentation? Should they be covered in the BBB?
 

 * Collision detection with the intercept register. How is it done? How are the different bits flagged and used?
 

 * Is there a definitive cartridge list?
 

 * What are UMARGT and USERTB and how are they used?
 

 * How are restart (RST) vectors used?
 

 * Custom system routines. This is a BIG one. Did any software ever use them? The NM is really dense on this point, so any clarifications would help. You can read what I have on this page http://metopal.com/projects/ballybook/doku.php?id=software:upi_conventions#custom_system_routines, but it's a bit cobbled together at this point.
 

 * In the Alternate Font Descriptor http://metopal.com/projects/ballybook/doku.php?id=software:alphanumeric#ix_alternate_font_descriptor, what is the 'base character'? I assumed it was the starting ASCII code for your custom character set, but I've found a weird anomaly with the small (3x5) character set. In the system ROM, its base character is $A0, but printing that character to screen yields garbage. However, bumping to $B0 prints the small characters as expected. Why?
 

 * What software used custom character sets? I'd love to see how this was implemented.
 

 * Lance Squire's 'Vector Animation' tutorial mentions two other tutorials: 'Flopping Around' and 'SENTRY'. Do they exist?
 

 OK, sorry, that's a lot, but I've dug into this system for dozens of hours now and I want to make the BBB a helpful, comprehensive resource. Any help or comments are useful and appreciated! Please send them my way.
 

 Nathan

    Since I'm off to vacation for a few days, I thought I'd post an update on the BBB. Most every bit of the NM is now transferred (except for the technical/electrical info near the end). Indeed, transferred, heavily revised and annotated. I'm really pleased with how the documentation is turning out, as I've been using it every day while I experiment around with Arcade programming.
Major segments have been rewritten or updated. The interrupts section now has far more description (and examples) of how screen interrupts function. I still don't fully grasp their practical use, but it's a good start (and they work in testing). I'm particularly proud of the alphanumeric display section. I spent a lot of time probing the system routines and figuring out how text is rendered. I put copious pictures, examples, an additional documentation there as well. Didn't understand ASCII control codes before? BBB has you covered.
Lots of tiny details too, like renaming sections and reorganizing content (e.g., Object Vectors instead of Screen Vectoring Routines) to clarify programming techniques. There are code snippets and a glossary too.
But I still have a ton to learn, and I could use some help on some technical details. Here's a few (well, a lot):
* I could really use some documentation for the BCD math routines. Their documentation is sparse, and I don't quite grok BCD math enough to write them on my own.BCD math takes the hexadecimal number used by the machine and translates it to the decimal system. BCD stands for Binary Coded Decimal.
* What is a 'SACRED register load'? This terminology is referenced in the SUCK and INDEXB routines, but I can't find clarification.There are 2 sets of registers you normally work within the Z-80 CPU. There is the normal working group:AF  BC  DE  and HL   and AF' BC' DE' and ' HL'   The second set is called the SACRED set of registers. The command  EXX exchanges these sets and makes the AF...AF" etc. this is one way to save some of the work you are doung and use a fresh group. Another EXX puts it all back.
* I think I get RELABS, but I'm not sure I understand its distinction from RELAB1.
* MSKTD is fairly mysterious as well. Any clarification on that routine would be helpful (beyond the 'Vector animation' tutorial, I mean), especially practical usage.MSKTD is used to mask out (or in) user inputs. by using it you can totally lock out any or all of the keypads keys. Some programmers have used it to lock out the HALT key so you can't stop the program and check it out while it is running.
* I haven't tackled expansion hardware at all. What's a good resource? What software used it and how?There have been several add on expansion units made for the Bally / Astrocade unit. There was the UV-1 (never made into production as also the ZGRASS unit didn't make it).Then there was the Blue Ram memory expansion unit. It was manufactured by Perkins Engineering. Sadly, both Clyde (hardware) and John (Software) Perkins have passed. It was made to have peripherals added to it's RAM.It started out as a 4K either DIY or have it made. It then went to a standard 16K unit and a premium 32K.It had a63 key keyboard available as well as a printer interface (Centronics interface) and a 300 baud modem interface.They also had a BSR home switching network similar to today's smart houses (only more archaic).It had it's own BASIC cartridge (originally on tape) called Blue RAM BASIC. That was derived from Jay Fenton's Hot Rod Bally BASIC. The major changes had to do with the I/O capabilities of the Blue RAM unit.
Next came the Viper and it's BASIC called ViperSoft. It was larger and had many of the same features as the Blue RAM. It's addressing scheme was the same as Hot Rod Bally BASIC. Alternative Engineering produced it.
Then came the unit designed by Mike White and myself. It was called the Lil' WHITE RAM. It was meant to plar ALL of the programs on the multi-carts. It has 32K of RAM.All 3 of these units had the ability of testing a machine language program as a cartridge and they each had write-protect capabilities.Lastly there was a 48K hybrid unit that only sold a few. I think it came too late, and was radically different. it had some FLASH RAM in it. I really don't know more about that unit.
* Interrupt scheduling. How is it managed, say for changed palette values as the screen is drawn? How did games use interrupts for timing? 
* Limitations. How many patterns can be drawn or vectored per frame / screen? How much does it take to bog down the Arcade?The main thing here is are they being drawn during Vertical interrupt or during standard execution time? there is only so mush avail time during V interrupt. The other limiting factor is the size of the graphics.
* Light pens. Were these commercially released? Used in software? Is there any extant documentation? Should they be covered in the BBB?sadly only a few were ever tried. The timing in the software made most not work right.
* Collision detection with the intercept register. How is it done? How are the different bits flagged and used?Basically, the DNA manual has the simplest version of this. It says that the Interrupt register tests to see if the unit has written anything to a previously turn "on" pixel. If so, then the interrupt  register is turned on. You need to "test" it to clear it.
* Is there a definitive cartridge list?The best list is those available on Bally Alley.
* What are UMARGT and USERTB and how are they used?
* How are restart (RST) vectors used?The RST vectors are addresses at the beginning of a cartridge. they are 2 BYTES ( 1 WORD) long. Then accessed thru the RST structure, it is used like a vector-type table. It looks at the WORD to see where the program should jump to. They are RST 00 (start the program from the start) RST 08, RST10, RST18, RST20, RST 28, RST 30, and RST 38 which starts you into the On Board Subroutine grogram.

* Custom system routines. This is a BIG one. Did any software ever use them? The NM is really dense on this point, so any clarifications would help. You can read what I have on this page, but it's a bit cobbled together at this point.Most of the original cartridges used them extensively. As programmers got better, they sometimes made their own because it would work faster than having to go thru the interpreter.
* In the Alternate Font Descriptor, what is the 'base character'? I assumed it was the starting ASCII code for your custom character set, but I've found a weird anomaly with the small (3x5) character set. In the system ROM, its base character is $A0, but printing that character to screen yields garbage. However, bumping to $B0 prints the small characters as expected. Why?There are no LETTERS associated with the small font in the Arcade unit.
* What software used custom character sets? I'd love to see how this was implemented.One good use of the font was in Black Jack.... Ie sae used extensively there.
* Lance Squire's 'Vector Animation' tutorial mentions two other tutorials: 'Flopping Around' and 'SENTRY'. Do they exist?Check the DNA manual for a description of FLOP.  SENTY also keeps track of the times and interupts as well as the description above.
OK, sorry, that's a lot, but I've dug into this system for dozens of hours now and I want to make the BBB a helpful, comprehensive resource. Any help or comments are useful and appreciated! Please send them my way.
Nathan

On 16-06-05 08:48 PM, ex_writer@yahoo.com [ballyalley] wrote:
...
>
> * I could really use some documentation for the BCD math routines. Their
> documentation is sparse, and I don't quite grok BCD math enough to write
> them on my own.
>

BCD (Binary Coded Decimal) is a way to store human readable numbers in a computer system.

Each nibble or half byte in BCD can have a value from 0-9 whereas normally accepts values 0-15 or 0-F hex.

As I understand it, the BCD math routines allow you to  add, subtract, etc these numbers without converting back to decimal/hex representation.

I believe the calculator function uses it, along with the original Bally BASIC. (It's in the early news letters.)


>
> * I think I get RELABS, but I'm not sure I understand its distinction
> from RELAB1.
>

RELABS converts X/Y to MAGIC RAM addresses plus sets the shift bits for the MAGIC register.

RELABS1 converts X/Y to SCREEN RAM addresses. Any pixel shifting is up to the user.

Both will FLOP the screen co-ordinates if indicated.


>
> * Limitations. How many patterns can be drawn or vectored per frame /
> screen? How much does it take to bog down the Arcade?
>

As the Bally doesn't have sprites or Character/Tile graphics, it has to do a lot of memory moves to draw anything on the screen.

The MAGIC functions of the hardware help by offloading pixel shifts, OR/XOR and expand functions from the CPU.

Someone will need to document how many bytes can be written to the screen within a standard Vertical blanking period.


>
> * Collision detection with the intercept register. How is it done? How
> are the different bits flagged and used?
>

I've been meaning to do a test on this for quite awhile. There is a report that it doesn't work exactly as advertised. However, Space Invaders/Astro Invaders uses it.


>
> * Custom system routines. This is a BIG one. Did any software ever use
> them?

The Wizard aka Wizard of WOR uses 6 or 7. You can look through the recent commented source code.


>
> * Lance Squire's 'Vector Animation' tutorial mentions two other
> tutorials: 'Flopping Around' and 'SENTRY'. Do they exist?
>

Flopping Around is/was started, but never released. I should get back to it.

The concepts I was covering are the two levels of FLOPping in the Bally/Astrocade. First as mentioned in the NM the bios does a full screen and controller FLOP. they use this for games like Gun Fight.

It allows you to make the graphics and code for the player on the left, as normal. But instead of making the graphics and modified movement code for the player on the right, you just set the FLOP bits and use the same code. The bios puts the image on the opposite side of the screen facing the right way, etc.

Good for head to head games.

The second is just using the hardware FLOPping. I use it in my skeleton demo to draw half the arm and leg images. Wizard also uses it for left(or was it right...) facing  sprites.

14484:
Longer explanation:

The * array holds the note values.

Encoded as A*100+B.

Line 20 splits the values and feeds Tone A and B

Line 30 puts Volume A & B at full then slides it down to 1. then sets it to -1 for reasons I don't know...

Lines 10 $ 40 operate the loops.

Line 30 is attempting to give the Bally sound an 'Envelope'. Something the Yamaha sound ships in the Vectrex, Spectravido, MSX, and Atari ST had. And the C64 in spades! While the BAlly, Atari 8bit, coco etc did not.

ML/assembler routines have been used in various systems to emulate sound envelopes with some success.

Nathan, are you aiming for this game to be small (with tightly-written routines) or useful as an example (with longer, easier-to-understand code)?  I'm guessing this will be a two-player game only?

I've always thought that a ML Pong-style game could be written in the RAM available to BASIC and then loaded with the :RUN command (rather than the :INPUT command, which loads a BASIC program).  This, of course, would require making the play screen narrower (as the game code would have to be at the bottom of the screen), but it would be a neat tech challenge.

Paul archived two early versions of the ICBM Attack cartridge by Spectre Systems.  These ML programs actually load from tape into AstroBASIC using the :RUN command. Crazy Climber is the main game for Round 9 of the Astrocade High Score Club. Since the library of Astrocade games is quite small, I've decided that rounds will no longer last just two weeks-- each round will be longer (usually three weeks). This will keep us from running out too quickly of cartridge games to play in each round. Round 9 will last three weeks. The round ends on Sunday, July 10'th at 8pm MST.

Overview of Crazy Climber:

The object of Crazy Climber is to reach the top of a nearly 200-story building. There are four buildings in total, each offering a variety of different challenges and obstacles that make the journey to the top more difficult.

Crazy Climber is an 8K homebrew game, released in 2011, by Riff Raff Games. This cartridge was written by Michael Garber.

Overview of Missile Defense:

This month's BASIC bonus game is called Missile Defense. It was released by New Image in 1982 on Tape 3. Also on Tape 3 was Saucer Attack, but that game is not being played this round. Here is a summary of Missile Defense gameplay from a New Image advertisement:

"Save your city from fallout! You have three chances to block the missile from hitting your city. Don't blow them!!! Intensity increases with score. Also saves initials of high scorer of the day."

If this game sounds suspiciously like a Missile Command clone, then you're correct! That's not a bad thing though, right?

For all the Round 9 details, see the thread on AtariAge in the Astrocade sub-forum:
